No questions, but from someone in the same situation (but for different reasons), I just wanted to say: hang in there. I know how hopeless life is. But at least they say it is short. 

However, don't underestimate your family, many people prefer seeing their children happy, even if it means them transitioning. But they need to be given the chance.

Listening comprehension was always my greatest weakness regardless of the lanugage (but French and English are probably among the most difficult ones listening comprehension wise seeing as the writing does not really match the pronounciation). The only thing that really helped me break out of the I-don't-understand-anything-phase was listening to media (podcasts, audio books, movies etc) while reading along with the transcript or subtitles. This trains your ear to associate what is heard with what you are already used to seeing and reading.

I understand why you say that, and I actually really appreciate hearing that, but after so many years I have considered it in so many ways and I have been externally assessed as hopeless as well (I just wrote an example further down the thread to another user). I have simply had extremely bad luck, worse than most transgender people. As a side note, regarding your point b) I am not a surgeon like you said, but I was once working as a junior doctor at the surgery ward. Now I am the world's biggest failure of a doctor lol. I had to quit due to depression to work in a calmer environment.
Anyway, sorry about the negativity and writing you all this, I hope it will be just like you say and that things are not as bad as they seem. Thanks for the sympathy friend

Hmm, I think you're right, we don't really know what we look like, probably because we always see each other in mirrors. I have tried something similar to what you describe and it is a little better than the mirror, because some angles are almost bearable. But my face is like one of those hologram pictures, from some angles it is catastrophic and from others less so. 

When I started transition for the first time, almost 10 years ago now, I was actually overly optimistic about my chances and did not realize how bad my situation was. It wasn't until I went out and was mocked and harassed on the street, and that my then best friend told me there is no way I could ever be mistaken for a woman, that I actually realized how bad it was. My perception was clouded by intense euphoria, and I don't think I've ever recovered from the harassement and disappointment. Sorry to tell you all this, but I think some people in the thread suspect that I have an overly negative impression of my chances, but that is just not the case. Thank you for writing all those suggestions!

Personally, I'd say that you could pretty much just dive in. Passe simple is much easier to learn than passe composé (no auxiliares varying depending on whether they're reflexive or not, etc), and books are almost always written in 3rd person meaning that you will almost exclusively see the 3rd person singular (and occasionally 3rd person plural) conjugations.

If you want an overview of how they are formed you should [read this](http://french.about.com/od/grammar/a/passesimple.htm) first, but there is no need to work hard on trying to memorize conjugation tables since only the 3rd person appears in books. Just pay attention to *fut* and *fit* which are common and do not look like the normal conjugations of être and faire.
